etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English yong, yonge, from Old English ġeong, from Proto-West Germanic *jung, from Proto-Germanic *jungaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuHn̥ḱós, from *h₂yuh₁en- (“young”).

definitions.definition: In the early part of growth or life; born not long ago.

quote.citation: 1809 October 26, William Wordsworth, “The French Revolution as It Appeared to Enthusiasts at Its Commencement”, in Friend, No. 11, ll. 4-5:
quote.text: Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive,But to be young was very heaven!
"What a charming amusement for young people this is, Mr. Darcy! There is nothing like dancing after all. I consider it as one of the first refinements of polished society."

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: I stumbled along through the young pines and huckleberry bushes. Pretty soon I struck into a sort of path that, I cal'lated, might lead to the road I was hunting for. It twisted and turned, and, the first thing I knew, made a sudden bend around a bunch of bayberry scrub and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn.
At Columbia-Greene, staffers go for the most unadoptable animals to save them from euthanasia. The youngest, healthiest, cutest pets are waiting for you.

quote.citation: 1998, Arne Gerdner, Compulsory Treatment for Alcohol Use Disorders, page 85:
quote.text: The factors related to increase in number of abscondings were younger age, psychiatric problems, multi-drug abuse and living alone.

quote.citation: 2013 July 19, Ian Sample, “Irregular bedtimes may affect children's brains”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 6, page 34:
quote.text: Irregular bedtimes may disrupt healthy brain development in young children, according to a study of intelligence and sleeping habits.  ¶ Going to bed at a different time each night affected girls more than boys, but both fared worse on mental tasks than children who had a set bedtime, researchers found.

definitions.definition: At an early stage of existence or development; having recently come into existence.

quote.citation: 1722, Daniel Defoe, A Journal of the Plague Year‎[1], London: E. Nutt et al, page 23:
quote.text: […]  while the Fears of the People were young, they were encreas’d strangely by several odd Accidents  […]

definitions.definition: (Not) advanced in age; (far towards or) at a specified stage of existence or age.

quote.citation: 1906, Robertson Nicoll, Tis Forty Years Since, quoted in T. P.'s Weekly, volume 8, page 462:
quote.text:
And thou, our Mother, twice two centuries young,
Bend with bright shafts of truth thy bow fresh-strung.

definitions.definition: Junior (of two related people with the same name).

quote.citation: 1841, The Museum of Foreign Literature, Science, and Art:
quote.text: The young Mr. Chester must be in the wrong, and the old Mr. Chester must be in the right.

quote.citation: 1922, E. Barrington, “The Mystery of Stella” in “The Ladies!” A Shining Constellation of Wit and Beauty, Boston: Atlantic Monthly Press, pp. 40-41,[2]
quote.text: […]  Miss Hessy is as pretty a girl as eye can see, in her young twenties and a bit of a fortune to boot.

quote.citation: 1965, Muriel Spark, The Mandelbaum Gate, London: Macmillan, Part One, Chapter 1:
quote.text: Ephraim would be in his young thirties.

quote.citation: 2008 January 20, Alice Fisher, “Grown-up chic is back as high street goes upmarket”, in The Guardian:
quote.text: […]  while this may appeal to older, better-off shoppers, vast numbers, especially those in their teens and young twenties, still want fast, cheap fashion.

definitions.definition: Youthful; having the look or qualities of a young person.

quote.citation: 2013 August 3, “Revenge of the nerds”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8847:
quote.text: Think of banking today and the image is of grey-suited men in towering skyscrapers. Its future, however, is being shaped in converted warehouses and funky offices in San Francisco, New York and London, where bright young things in jeans and T-shirts huddle around laptops, sipping lattes or munching on free food.

definitions.definition: Of or belonging to the early part of life.
(obsolete) Having little experience; inexperienced; unpracticed; ignorant; weak.

quote.citation: c. 1598–1600 (date written), William Shakespeare, “As You Like It”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: Come, come, elder brother, you are too young in this.

definitions.definition: (often as if a plural noun) Offspring, especially the immature offspring of animals.

quote.citation: 2010, Mammal Anatomy: An Illustrated Guide‎[3], page 21:
quote.text: There is a logic in this behavior: a mother will not come into breeding condition again unless her young is ready to be weaned or has died, so killing a baby may hasten  […]

definitions.definition: (informal or demography) To become or seem to become younger.

quote.citation: 1993, Jacob S. Siegel, A Generation of Change, page 5:
quote.text: The aging (or younging) of a population refers to the fact that a population, as a unit of observation, is getting older (or younger).

definitions.definition: (informal or demography) To cause to appear younger.

quote.citation: 1984, US Bureau of the Census, Current Population Reports‎[4], page 74:
quote.text: Medicare data was "younged" by a month to achieve conformity with the conventional completed ages recorded in the census.

quote.citation: 1994, R. Kerrich, D.A. Wyman, “The mesothermal gold-lamprophyre association”, in Mineralogy and Petrology, →DOI:
quote.text: Shoshonitic magmatism younged southwards in the Superior Province, commensurate with the southwardly diachronous accretion of allochthonous subprovinces.

quote.citation: 2001 November 23, Paul Tapponnier et al., “Oblique Stepwise Rise and Growth of the Tibet Plateau”, in Science‎[5], volume 294, number 5547, →DOI, pages 1671–1677:
quote.text: The existence of magmatic belts younging northward implies that slabs of Asian mantle subducted one after another under ranges north of the Himalayas.
